card.h1: You don't need a spa. You need a better night.
card.p: Stillwater Rooms — a wellness program built for boutique hotels of 20 to 80 keys

card.h1: Your guest checked in already exhausted

ul.li: "Rest and recharge" is now the number one stated motivation for leisure travel, cited by 56% of travelers
Spending time in nature (37%) and improving mental health (36%) follow it — ahead of sightseeing or nightlife
More than one in four travelers plan to take a solo trip, and 48% intend to add solo days around family travel
The industry has a name for it now: hushpitality — the quietcation, the digital detox, luxury defined by what's been removed

card.p: The guest who used to ask what's nearby now asks how quiet the room is.

card.h1: Sleep is the only amenity every single guest uses

ul.li: A spa treatment needs a booking, a time slot, and a guest who wants to undress. Sleep needs none of that — it applies equally to the business traveler, the couple, and the exhausted parent
36% of American adults get insufficient rest, and sleep tourism has grown into a sector valued above $690 billion, with roughly $400 billion of further growth projected to 2028
Guests are now literate about the levers — light, temperature, sound, mattress support, air quality, screen exposure — which means they can evaluate you on them

card.p: It is the one wellness product with a 100% addressable audience and no scheduling friction.

card.h1: The trap is thinking the answer is a spa

ul.li: Treatment rooms are expensive real estate. Industry benchmarks put revenue at roughly $111,000 per treatment room annually in upper-upscale hotels — a number that only works at scale you don't have
The capture is thinner than it looks. Spa revenue per occupied room averages about $18 in upper-upscale properties versus $40 in luxury
Payroll is the killer. Hotels with major wellness operations post the strongest total revenue, but their cost structure — the payroll burden in particular — continues to weigh on profitability

card.p: A 42-key hotel that builds two treatment rooms has bought itself a department, a rota, and a licensing problem.

card.h1: In 2025, the small programs started beating the big ones
Minor wellness overtook major wellness on every line that matters

ul.li: ADR: $250 for minor wellness properties versus $232 for major wellness
RevPAR: $170 versus $161 — minor wellness ahead in absolute terms
GOPPAR: $99 versus $89 — the first time minor wellness has led on operating profit

card.p: All three moved in favor of the smaller programs simultaneously for the first time, on data covering more than 12,000 properties. The reading is structural: a leaner cost base converts revenue to profit better than a bigger facility does.

card.h1: Curation is the boutique advantage, not a consolation prize

ul.li: Wellness isn't a niche you're late to — the wellness economy reached $6.8 trillion in 2024 and is forecast to hit $9.8 trillion by 2029
Wellness tourism alone accounted for $894 billion of spend in 2024

For a small property, the ancillary model is product placement, retail, and experience partnerships rather than F&B volume or spa capacity — one well-chosen partnership can add £15–£40 per stay while reinforcing the brand that justifies the rate

card.p: You are not competing with a resort spa. You are competing with the guest's own bedroom — and winning that is cheaper than you think.

card.h1: Three layers, none of which is a construction project

ul.li: The Room. A specified sleep environment in every key — the physical product, delivered once.
The Rhythm. A weekly cadence of rituals run by vetted local practitioners on revenue share, not payroll.
The Ledger. Bookable packages, priced and loaded into your booking engine, so the program shows up as revenue rather than as goodwill.

card.p: No treatment rooms. No new department. No licensed-practitioner headcount on your P&L.

card.h1: Layer one — the room, specified to six levers

ul.li: Light: blackout to under 1 lux at the pillow, plus a 2200K bedside lamp that doesn't suppress melatonin
Sound: door sweeps and a white-noise unit, targeting a measured 30 dBA at the bed
Temperature: thermostat pre-set to 18.5°C at turndown, with a cooling and a warming duvet weight offered at booking
Surface: a mattress topper and pillow menu of three densities, chosen at check-in rather than requested later
Air: a quiet HEPA unit per room, filters on a logged 90-day cycle
Screens: a charging drawer outside arm's reach of the bed, and an analog alarm clock so the phone has no excuse

card.p: Every lever is measurable, so the promise on your website is one you can audit.

card.h1: Layer two — the rhythm, without the rota

ul.li: Four sessions a week, run in space you already have: a lobby corner at 7am, a courtyard, a roof terrace
A fixed cadence guests can plan around — sunrise breathwork Tuesday and Friday, restorative stretch Wednesday, a Sunday sound bath
Practitioners are contracted, not employed. Stillwater sources, vets, insures and schedules them; they're paid a share of session revenue, so an empty session costs you nothing
Your front desk sells it with a one-line script at check-in and a card on the bed — no new system to learn

card.p: The fixed variable cost of layer two is zero. That is the whole point of the model.

card.h1: Layer three — the ledger, so it reads as revenue

ul.li: The Quiet Night package — room upgrade to full sleep specification, turndown ritual, and a late 2pm checkout, sold as a rate add-on
Session passes — single-session drop-in or a stay-length pass, bookable at reservation or at the desk
The takeaway kit — sleep mask, magnesium balm, a caffeine-free tea blend, and the room's own pillow spray, at retail margin
Reporting — a monthly one-page read on attach rate, session fill, retail per occupied room, and the ADR delta between program and non-program stays

card.p: If it isn't measured against your existing KPIs, it will be cut in the first soft quarter. So we measure it against them from week one.

card.h1: A worked example: The Ardmore, 42 keys
card.p: Illustrative example. Stillwater Rooms and The Ardmore are fictional, created for this prototype. The figures below are a transparent model built from the stated assumptions — not results from a real client, and not a forecast of yours.

ul.li: Assumptions: 42 keys, 70% annual occupancy, $265 ADR → 10,731 occupied room-nights
Quiet Night package: $85, at a 12% attach rate → 1,288 packages → $109,480
Sessions: 4 per week × 52 weeks, averaging 5 paying guests at $25 → $26,000
Retail: $3.50 per occupied room-night → $37,559
Less practitioner share (55% of sessions, $14,300), retail cost of goods (45%, $16,902), and program fee ($3,200/mo, $38,400)
Net contribution: ≈ $103,400 against a one-time fit-out of ≈ $26,000 — payback inside four months

card.p: Change the attach rate to 8% and it still clears $65,000. The model is yours to stress-test before you sign anything.

card.h1: It should sound like your hotel, not like a franchise

ul.li: An independent property's advantage is that its program can be specific to place — rooted in local traditions, local ingredients, local practitioners — where a chain's wellness offer is designed by a corporate team for replicability across markets
That differentiation is what enables pricing power and loyalty that commodity wellness cannot achieve
So we source locally by default: your tea blend from a regional producer, your balm from a maker within 100 miles, your practitioners from your own city
And we write it in your voice. We supply the structure and the standards; the naming, the copy, and the rituals are built with your team in the onboarding workshop

card.h1: What it costs and how we get paid

ul.li: One-time fit-out: roughly $550–$700 per key, covering the six levers, installed over a low-occupancy week. You own the hardware outright.
Program fee: a flat monthly retainer scaled to key count — sourcing, practitioner management, insurance, training, collateral, and monthly reporting
Practitioner revenue share: paid out of session revenue only, so it never touches fixed cost
No lock-in: a 12-month initial term, then 60 days' notice. If you leave, the rooms, the supplier relationships, and the training stay with you

card.p: We'd rather earn the renewal than litigate the exit.

card.h1: Ninety days from signature to first Quiet Night sold

ol.li: Days 1–14 — Audit. We measure light, sound, and temperature in a sample of your rooms, and pull twelve months of your ADR and occupancy to set a real baseline
Days 15–35 — Design. Onboarding workshop with your GM and front-desk lead: naming, pricing, the local supplier shortlist, and practitioner interviews
Days 36–60 — Install. Fit-out scheduled into your softest week, floor by floor, no rooms out of inventory for more than one night each
Days 61–75 — Train and load. Front-desk scripts, the booking-engine rate plan, photography, and a soft launch to your repeat guests
Days 76–90 — Open and measure. Full launch, first monthly report, and the first attach-rate review against baseline

card.h1: The four questions every GM asks us

ul.li: "What if the sessions don't fill?" They cost you nothing when they don't — practitioners are paid from session revenue. We review cadence at day 90 and drop what isn't working.
"Will this disrupt housekeeping?" The turndown ritual adds roughly 90 seconds per room and is trained in a single shift. The air filters are on a 90-day log, not a daily task.
"Our rooms are small." Good. Every lever is in-room and takes no floor area. The sessions run in space you already own and don't currently monetize.
"Can we start with one floor?" Yes — a 10-key pilot with the same measurement, converting to full rollout or walking away at 120 days.

card.h1: Give us one floor and ninety days

ul.li: The ask: a 10-key pilot, audit starting within three weeks
What you commit: the fit-out for ten rooms, one workshop morning from your GM, and a front-desk briefing
What you get back: a measured attach rate, a real ADR delta against your own baseline, and a decision you can make on numbers rather than on a pitch
Walk away at 120 days and you keep the rooms, the suppliers, and the data

card.p: The guest is already asking for a quieter night. The only question is whether they're paying you for it.

brief.instruction: Confident, plain, commercially literate — you are talking to a hotel GM or owner-operator who reads a P&L every month and has been pitched before. Sentence case throughout. About 55 words per slide, mostly bulleted; the template holds roughly 55 words a card, so budget 55 and go higher only on the worked-example slide, which is deliberately dense because its whole value is that the reader can check the arithmetic. Specifics over adjectives: name the number, the lever, the timeframe. Never write "elevate", "transform", "holistic", "journey", "seamless", or "unlock". Avoid the word "solution". Vary sentence and paragraph length. Never the "Bold term: explanation" pattern as a whole-slide format — the bold lead-ins in this outline are deliberate and limited to list rows that genuinely pair a label with a value. No signposting ("Let's explore", "In this section"). No sweeping openers or inspirational closers — start and end on substance. None of the "not just X — it's Y" contrast family. No em dashes in body copy. Keep every figure exactly as written in the outline. The arithmetic on the worked-example slide must stay internally consistent; do not round, restate, or "improve" any number.

Clean white and soft teal, polished but welcoming — warmer and more hospitable than a corporate pitch, calmer than a spa brochure. The template's pale architectural grounds and frosted planes carry that well; use the teal accent sparingly, once per card, most often as the rule under a lead figure. Imagery is boutique-hotel and rest, shot like a hospitality brand rather than a stock wellness library: an unmade bed in early daylight, blackout linen against a bright window, a lobby corner set for a morning session, a courtyard at dawn, a takeaway kit laid out on stone. Real interiors and materials, natural light, no people mid-yoga-pose, no lotus hands, no candles-and-pebbles clichés, no visible branding on props. Give the proof slides room to land. The minor-versus-major wellness comparison deserves a genuine chart treatment with the three paired figures legible at a glance. The worked-example slide is the deck's centerpiece and should read as a clean financial ledger, not a bulleted list — a table or structured figure layout so a GM can scan the arithmetic line by line. The 90-day rollout wants a real sequence treatment. The three-layer overview slide should show the three layers as distinct blocks, and the following three slides each expand one of them, so the visual relationship between them is explicit. Both chapter-title cards are dark-field breaks — use them for pace, and keep the two closing slides sparse.

This deck was built for a prototype with no company data, client assets, or source document supplied. Stillwater Rooms (the provider) and The Ardmore (the 42-key example property) are invented for illustration. The worked-example slide carries a single explicit label saying so; keep that label exactly where it is and do not repeat the disclaimer on other slides. Do not invent anything beyond what the outline contains: no client names, no testimonials, no case-study outcomes, no "hotels using Stillwater saw X", no logos, no photographs presented as a real property, no awards or certifications. The pricing, fit-out costs, and revenue lines are a transparent model built from stated assumptions and must never be phrased as achieved results. The cited market and benchmark figures are real and sourced. Reproduce them exactly as written, keep each one attached to the claim it supports, and do not extrapolate from them or add a statistic that is not in the outline.
